clinicalPearls: A testis that intermittently withdraws from the scrotum into the groin due to an overactive cremasteric reflex, but can be brought down and stays in the scrotum
It is a normal variant in prepubertal boys and must be distinguished from a truly undescended (cryptorchid) testis
The key clinical feature is that the testis, once manipulated into the scrotum, remains there without tension until the reflex is re-triggered
The cremasteric reflex is most active in mid-childhood, when retractile testes are commonest
A minority become ascending (acquired undescended) testes over time, so periodic review is advised
No surgery is needed for a genuinely retractile testis, but an ascending testis requires orchidopexy
reference.pathophysiology: A retractile testis results from a brisk cremasteric reflex that pulls a normally descended testis up toward the external ring, particularly with cold or handling. Because the spermatic cord is of adequate length, the testis can be drawn back into and remain in the scrotum, distinguishing it from cryptorchidism. In some boys relative shortening of the cord with growth converts a retractile testis into an ascending (acquired undescended) testis, which no longer stays down.
additionalInvestigations: Careful examination in a warm, relaxed setting to overcome the cremasteric reflex
Confirmation that the testis stays in the scrotum after manipulation
Serial follow-up to detect an ascending testis
Referral if the testis cannot be kept in the scrotum
redFlags: A testis that will not stay in the scrotum (undescended/ascending)
Loss of a previously scrotal testis on follow-up
reference.prognosis: A truly retractile testis is benign and typically resolves at puberty, but the small risk of progression to an ascending testis warrants monitoring.
pitfalls: Labelling an undescended or ascending testis as merely retractile
Examining in a cold or anxious setting and misjudging position
Failing to arrange follow-up for possible ascent
Reassuring without confirming the testis stays down
management: Reassure that a genuinely retractile testis is a normal variant needing no surgery
Confirm the diagnosis by examining in a warm, relaxed setting and demonstrating that the testis stays in the scrotum after manipulation
Arrange periodic clinical review through childhood to detect conversion to an ascending (acquired undescended) testis
Refer for orchidopexy if the testis can no longer be maintained in the scrotum
Avoid routine imaging, which does not aid management
Reassess around puberty, when the cremasteric reflex wanes and retraction typically resolves
